confounds: Diagnosed users were more active: median timeline size was about 408 posts versus 334 for controls, with means about 627 versus 530. Any-hit prevalence can therefore be inflated; per-user post-rate normalization reduced but did not eliminate this concern.
Mental-health terms are polysemous and may represent self-report, treatment access, advocacy, jokes, lyrics, quotations, news, or discussion of someone else.
The context filters were heuristic and cannot perfectly separate first-person experience from third-person or quoted material.
Fold-to-fold variation was largest for rare suicidality/self-harm language and isolation language, consistent with sampling sensitivity.
The corpus contains only labels, source fold, and retained posts; no timestamps or demographic metadata are available to separate duration, life-stage, event, or cohort effects.
The diagnosed/control imbalance is substantial: 618 diagnosed versus 5,463 control users, so rare-feature estimates have limited precision.
All findings are observational associations with labels and should not be interpreted as clinical diagnosis, severity, or causal mechanisms.

caveats: Terms can reflect help-seeking, advocacy, ordinary anxiety, metaphor, or discussion of another person.

findings.evidence_summary: Strongest low-level divergence. The gap remained positive in every development fold, approximately 24.4 to 32.2 percentage points. Treatment-related language was also substantially enriched.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use as a high-value but non-diagnostic feature. Prefer user-level prevalence and normalized rates, and require context and persistence rather than isolated keywords.

negative_results: Broad self-evaluation/helplessness lexicons were nearly universal: about 99% of both classes, with only +1.6 to +1.8 percentage points for diagnosed users; weak standalone signals.
Low-energy/sleep vocabulary was common in both groups (90.8% diagnosed vs 83.4% control; +7.4 pp) and had small normalized-rate separation, so it should be downweighted alone.
Generic mortality vocabulary was not fold-stable: diagnosed-minus-control gaps were approximately +4.8, -2.8, +3.8, and +5.4 pp across folds.
Positive-affect vocabulary was not reduced among diagnosed users; it appeared in 99.8% diagnosed vs 98.4% control users, cautioning against a simple negative-valence interpretation.
Sports/fandom vocabulary showed essentially no class separation overall (87.9% diagnosed vs 87.2% control) and mixed fold directions.
